title: SSTable and LSM Tree Production Review

questions.question: What is the core on-disk invariant of an SSTable?
options: Records are mutable and stored in insertion order
Records are immutable and sorted by key
Every key has a full in-memory index entry
Every write immediately updates all levels
questions.explanation: An SSTable is written once and keeps records in key order. Immutability enables sequential creation and checksums; sorting enables sparse indexes and ordered scans.

questions.question: Why must an LSM-tree write usually reach the WAL before the system acknowledges it?
options: The WAL sorts the final SSTable blocks
The MemTable is volatile and needs a durable replay source
The WAL eliminates every future compaction
The Bloom filter can only read WAL records
questions.explanation: The MemTable provides fast sorted memory writes but does not survive a crash. The WAL supplies the durable sequence needed to reconstruct accepted changes.

questions.question: A Bloom filter reports that a key is absent from an SSTable. What may the read path conclude?
options: The key is definitely absent from that SSTable
The key is definitely present in the block cache
The key exists but has expired
The sparse index is corrupt
questions.explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives when implemented correctly. A negative result safely skips the table; a positive result is only a maybe.

questions.question: Why does a range scan not receive the same benefit from a point-key Bloom filter?
options: Ranges are never sorted
The filter answers membership for one key, not whether any key falls inside an interval
Range scans cannot use sparse indexes
The block cache is disabled for scans
questions.explanation: A point-key filter can reject one exact key. It does not summarize arbitrary interval overlap, so range scans still inspect the runs and blocks whose key bounds overlap the requested interval.

questions.question: Writes arrive at 100 MB/s and the strategy has 6x total write amplification. Approximately how much background rewrite capacity is required by this lesson's model?
options: 100 MB/s
500 MB/s
600 MB/s of additional logical writes
6 MB/s
questions.explanation: The initial flush accounts for one copy. The remaining 5x represents background rewrite work, so 100 x (6 - 1) is about 500 MB/s.

questions.question: Which condition most directly signals compaction debt?
options: The sparse index fits in memory
Required compaction work stays above background compaction capacity
The WAL is appended sequentially
A negative Bloom lookup returns quickly
questions.explanation: A sustained throughput deficit makes immutable runs accumulate. Read amplification, space use, and flush pressure then worsen even when foreground writes still appear healthy.

questions.question: What is the safest recovery response when an SSTable checksum fails during a read?
options: Return the bytes anyway because the file is immutable
Rewrite the block in place
Quarantine the file and restore or rebuild from a verified replica or durable source
Disable checksums for future reads
questions.explanation: Immutability makes in-place repair the wrong boundary. The system should stop serving corrupt data, identify the affected file, and recover from trusted replicated or replayable state.
